lesson.title: Opening the Door: The Listen Operation
lesson.summary: The listen operation switches a bound TCP socket into a passive state that is willing to accept incoming connections, backed by a queue that holds connections until the application is ready to accept them.
lesson.body:
listen() is the sockets API call that switches a bound TCP socket from an idle state into one that is actively willing to accept incoming connection attempts from clients. It is specific to TCP in practice, since a UDP socket has no notion of a connection to accept in the first place, it just receives independent datagrams.

listen() takes a backlog argument, which is roughly the maximum number of connections the operating system should hold in a queue, connections that have completed or are in the process of completing the TCP handshake, while the application has not yet gotten around to calling accept() for them. Before listen() is ever called, a socket might already be bound to an address, but any client attempting to connect() to it at that point would get nothing useful in return, no response, or an outright connection refused or reset error, since nothing on that end is actually prepared to carry out a handshake yet.

The reason this queue exists is that an application does not always call accept() the very instant a client shows up, it might still be busy handling a previous client's request. Incoming connections wait in this backlog queue until the server's loop gets back around to calling accept() for each of them in turn. If that backlog ever fills up because the server cannot keep up with the rate of incoming attempts, further connection attempts are typically dropped or refused until space opens up again, which is one reason an overloaded server can start turning away new clients even though it is technically still running.

listen() only makes sense on a socket that has already been bound to a socket address, the subject of the previous chapter, since clients need a known, fixed address to attempt a connection to in the first place. And listen() is itself what sets up the state that the next operation, accept(), depends on to have anything to retrieve.
